synopsis: Peru uses national workplace and mining regulation rather than a continent-wide South American machinery regime [f2285]. Its DS 024-2016-EM is in force and provides a general mining occupational safety and mobile-equipment risk framework [f2803, f2132, f2294, f15584]. The reviewed material did not reveal a dedicated collision-braking acceptance regime; this is a finding about the review, not proof that such requirements do not exist [f2295, f15585, f2297, f15586]. Numeric acceptance items are explicitly reported as “not found,” not “not required,” for Peru and the other named South American countries [f2297, f15586]. The booklet also found no dedicated off-road rule in Peru requiring an ML-based collision-avoidance function to meet a specified ML validation standard by 2028 [f2393].

relations.note: Both report no collision-braking acceptance regime found in the reviewed Peruvian regulation.
Both define DS 024-2016-EM as mining occupational safety regulation with a general risk framework.
The latter specifies the occupational safety and mobile-equipment scope of the general mining rules.
Both distinguish numeric items not found from not required; the glossary names fewer countries.
The glossary clarifies that missing acceptance requirements cannot be treated as unnecessary.
Peru's mining regulation is a specific example of the regional reliance on national rules.
The latter confirms that the described Peruvian regulation is in force.
